title: Printing with std::cout
summary: Write your first C++ program and print text and numbers to the console with std::cout.
intro: Every program talks to you through its output. In C++ that starts with `std::cout`, the `#include` line that brings it in, and a complete `main` function.

steps.title: Your first program

example.title: Welcome banner
example.prompt: Print a three line welcome banner, one statement per line.
example.output:
Welcome to Hack University
Lesson 1: Printing
Let's write C++!
example.explanation: `#include <iostream>` makes `std::cout` available. Each statement sends a string literal into `std::cout`, then the char literal `'\n'` to end the line. The three statements run top to bottom, so the lines appear in that order. The apostrophe in `Let's` is fine inside double quotes. `return 0;` reports success.

practice.title: Course card
practice.prompt:
Print a three line card for a course.

1. Print `Course: Data Structures`
2. Print `Language: C++17`
3. Print `Status: Enrolled`
4. Use one `std::cout` statement per line, each ending in `<< '\n'`.

Expected output:

```text
Course: Data Structures
Language: C++17
Status: Enrolled
```

tests.output:
Course: Data Structures
Language: C++17
Status: Enrolled

hints: Copy the shape of the example: `std::cout << "text" << '\n';`
Write three statements above `return 0;`, one for each line, and do not forget the semicolons.

steps.title: Printing numbers and line breaks
steps.body:
`std::cout` prints numbers too. Write them without quotes and chain them between text pieces. Put the spaces inside the text, because `<<` adds none of its own.

```cpp
std::cout << "Score: " << 42 << '\n';     // Score: 42
std::cout << "Price: " << 2.5 << '\n';    // Price: 2.5
```

Whole numbers like `42` are integer literals. Numbers with a point like `2.5` are decimal (floating-point) literals. By default `std::cout` drops trailing zeros, so `2.50` prints as `2.5` and `3.0` prints as `3`. It also shows at most 6 significant digits, so `3.14159265` prints as `3.14159`. A later lesson shows how to control decimal places.

A string literal can hold `\n` itself, so one statement can print several lines: `std::cout << "Line 1\nLine 2\n";`.

`std::endl` also ends a line, but it then *flushes* the stream, forcing buffered output out right away. Flushing is slow when repeated, so prefer `'\n'` and save `std::endl` for when output must appear immediately.

example.title: Game status
example.prompt: Print a game status by chaining text with number literals, print two lines from one string, and finish with std::endl.
example.output:
Level 3 of 10
Health: 95.5
Start
Go
Done
example.explanation: The first statement chains four pieces: text, the integer `3`, text, the integer `10`. The spaces live inside `"Level "` and `" of "`. The decimal literal `95.5` prints exactly as written. The third statement prints two lines because its string contains two `\n` characters. `std::endl` ends the last line and flushes the output.

practice.title: Elevator status
practice.prompt:
Print a short elevator status report.

1. Print `Floor 7 of 12` by chaining text with the number literals `7` and `12`.
2. Print `Temperature: 21.5` by chaining text with the decimal literal `21.5`.
3. Print `Ready` and `Set` on two lines from a single statement, using `\n` inside the string.
4. Print `Go!` and end that line with `std::endl`.

Expected output:

```text
Floor 7 of 12
Temperature: 21.5
Ready
Set
Go!
```

tests.output:
Floor 7 of 12
Temperature: 21.5
Ready
Set
Go!

hints: Numbers go outside the quotes, the same way the example chains `"Level " << 3`.
Remember the spaces inside the text pieces, since `<<` adds none.
For the two lines, put a `\n` after each word inside one string literal.

steps.title: Comments, escapes, and raw strings
steps.body:
Comments are notes for people, and the compiler ignores them. `//` comments out the rest of the line. `/* ... */` can span several lines.

Some characters cannot be typed directly inside a string literal, so you write an *escape sequence* that starts with a backslash:

| Escape | Prints |
| --- | --- |
| `\"` | a double quote |
| `\\` | one backslash |
| `\n` | a newline |
| `\t` | a tab |

```cpp
std::cout << "Say \"yes\"" << '\n';   // Say "yes"
std::cout << "a\\b" << '\n';          // a\b
```

A lone backslash always starts an escape. `"C:\new"` prints a newline in the middle, and `"C:\Users"` does not even compile because `\U` starts a Unicode escape. Tabs are invisible, so this course keeps `\t` out of checked output.

A *raw string literal* skips escapes. Everything between `R"(` and `)"` is kept exactly as typed, backslashes and quotes included:

```cpp
std::cout << R"(C:\temp\new)" << '\n';  // C:\temp\new
```

example.title: Quotes and paths
example.prompt: Print a quoted phrase and a Windows path with escape sequences, then print the path again from a raw string.
example.explanation: The block comment at the top and the `//` comments are skipped by the compiler, so they print nothing. In `"She said \"hi\""` each `\"` becomes one quote character, and the unescaped quote at the end closes the string. In the second statement each `\\` becomes one backslash. The raw string `R"(C:\Users\guest)"` needs no escapes and prints the same path.

practice.title: File and path
practice.prompt:
Print a file name and a path, first with escapes and then with a raw string.

1. Print `The file is "notes.txt"` using `\"` for the quotes.
2. Print `D:\code\main.cpp` using `\\` for each backslash.
3. Print the same path again from a raw string literal.
4. Put a `//` comment above each of the three statements.

Expected output:

```text
The file is "notes.txt"
D:\code\main.cpp
D:\code\main.cpp
```
hints: Inside normal quotes write `\"` for a quote and `\\` for a backslash.
A raw string looks like `R"(text)"`, and the backslashes inside stay single.

recap:
- `#include <iostream>` brings in `std::cout`, and every program runs from `int main()` and ends with `return 0;`.
- `std::cout << "text" << '\n';` prints a line. Chain as many `<<` pieces as you like, and end each statement with a semicolon.
- Double quotes hold text (`"Hi"`), single quotes hold one character (`'\n'`).
- Write numbers without quotes: `42`, `2.5`. Put spaces inside the text pieces.
- `\n` can sit inside a string. `std::endl` ends the line and flushes, so prefer `'\n'`.
- `//` and `/* */` are comments. `\"`, `\\`, and `\t` are escapes, and `R"(...)"` keeps backslashes as typed.
